propositions.text: This is an application for leave and judicial review under section 72(1) of IRPA of the RPD decision dated November 7, 2016.
propositions.quote: This is an application for leave and judicial review under section 72(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 (the “Act” or “IRPA”) of the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (“RPD”), dated November 7, 2016

propositions.text: The RPD determined that the Applicant was neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection based on lack of credibility.
propositions.quote: wherein the RPD determined that Yongqiang Zhu (the “Applicant”) was neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection under sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA on the basis that the Applicant was not credible.

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review application of the RPD decision that found the Applicant not credible and not a refugee or person in need of protection.

propositions.text: The Applicant is a Chinese citizen born in 1994, a farmer with limited education from Heibei Province.
propositions.quote: The Applicant is a citizen of China, born on December 4, 1994. He alleges that he is a farmer with a limited education from Heibei Province, China.

propositions.text: He was introduced to Falun Gong practice by a friend and became a practitioner with friends.
propositions.quote: On January 7, 2014, the Applicant states that he was introduced to the practice of Falun Gong by a friend Li, Yongqi and that he thereafter became a practitioner along with his friends Zhu, Hongwei and Zhu, Hongtao.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant says he is a Chinese farmer born in 1994 who began practicing Falun Gong with friends in 2014.

propositions.text: On February 18, 2016, the Applicant's Falun Gong group was raided by the PSB; he was not present and learned from a friend.
propositions.quote: On February 18, 2016, the Applicant’s Falun Gong practice group was raided by the Chinese Public Security Bureau (“PSB”). The Applicant was not at practice that day, and allegedly received this information from Zhu, Hongwei.

propositions.text: After the raid, the Applicant went into hiding; PSB officers went to his home that night.
propositions.quote: As a result, the Applicant went into hiding. That night, PSB officers allegedly went to the Applicant’s home.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant says his Falun Gong group was raided in 2016, he went into hiding, and PSB officers visited his home that night.

propositions.text: On July 5, 2016, the Applicant left China with a snakehead's help, flew to Vancouver, then Toronto.
propositions.quote: On July 5, 2016, the Applicant exited China with the assistance of a snakehead and took a plane to Vancouver. The same day that he landed in Vancouver, the Applicant flew to Toronto.

propositions.text: His visa was cancelled around July 19, 2016, due to a group member's refugee claim.
propositions.quote: On or about July 19, 2016, the Applicant’s visa was cancelled because a member of the group with whom he was travelling, according to his visa, made a refugee claim.

propositions.text: On or about August 8, 2016, the Applicant claimed refugee protection in Canada fearing harm if returned to China for Falun Gong practice.
propositions.quote: On or about August 8, 2016, the Applicant also made a claim for refugee protection in Canada, based on fears that he will be arrested, incarcerated, and physically harmed by the PSB, should he be returned to China, because he is a Falun Gong practitioner.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant left China in July 2016 with a snakehead, had his visa cancelled, and claimed refugee protection fearing persecution for Falun Gong.

propositions.text: The RPD found the Applicant was neither a Convention refugee nor in need of protection due to negative credibility findings.
propositions.quote: The RPD held that the Applicant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, and rejected the Applicant’s claim based on a number of negative credibility findings.

propositions.text: RPD's reasons included: (a) Applicant exited China on own passport despite being wanted; (b) no documentation of PSB visits to parents; (c) delayed refugee claim; (d) prior US visa misrepresentation; (e) unconvincing Falun Gong practice details and no supporting evidence.
propositions.quote: a) The Applicant exited from China via the Beijing airport, travelling on his own passport and with a boarding pass issued in his name, while allegedly wanted by the Chinese Authorities; b) The Applicant was unable to provide any documentation of the alleged visits to his parents by the PSB; c) The Applicant did not claim refugee protection upon his arrival at the Toronto Airport, instead waiting over a month to make his claim; d) In 2013, the Applicant misrepresented himself in a United States visa application. e) The Applicant’s Falun Gong practice details were not compelling and there was no evidence tendered to support his claims of practicing Falun Gong in China or Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD rejected the Applicant's refugee claim due to multiple negative credibility findings including travel on own passport and lack of evidence.

propositions.text: The RPD found cumulative negative credibility findings undermined the Applicant's overall credibility and trustworthiness.
propositions.quote: In light of the negative credibility findings against the Applicant, the RPD held that the cumulative effect undermined the credibility of the Applicant in general.

propositions.text: No witnesses or witness testimonials were presented to support the Applicant's claim.
propositions.quote: Further, there were no witnesses called and there were no witness testimonials tendered.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD concluded the Applicant was not credible overall and noted no supporting witnesses or testimonials were presented.

propositions.text: The sole issue is whether the RPD's credibility findings are reasonable.
propositions.quote: The only issue is whether the credibility findings made by the RPD are reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the issue as the reasonableness of the RPD's credibility findings.

propositions.text: The applicable standard of review is reasonableness, citing Diaz v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration).
propositions.quote: The applicable standard of review is reasonableness (Diaz v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 1343 at para 10 [Diaz]).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the standard of review is reasonableness, citing Diaz.

propositions.text: The court finds the RPD's credibility findings reasonable and dismisses the application.
propositions.quote: I find that the credibility findings made by the RPD are reasonable, pursuant to section 107(2) of the IRPA. For the reasons below, the application is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD's credibility findings reasonable and dismisses the application.

propositions.text: The RPD drew a negative credibility inference from the Applicant exiting China via Beijing airport on his own passport while allegedly wanted.
propositions.quote: The RPD drew a negative credibility inference from the Applicant’s claim that he was wanted by the PSB at the time that he exited China, because the evidence submitted by the Applicant showed that he departed China via Beijing airport using a genuine passport issued in his own name.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found it not credible that the Applicant exited China on his own passport while wanted by authorities.

propositions.text: The Applicant argues the RPD erred in drawing a negative inference about exiting China on his own passport, citing Zhang 2008 for bribery plausibility.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the RPD erred in drawing a negative inference based on his ability to exit China using his own genuine passport. The Applicant relies upon jurisprudence from the Court for the proposition that there is nothing implausible about a person, who is wanted by the PSB, being able to exit China on his or her own genuine passport, in situations where the appropriate official was bribed: see Zhang v Canada, 2008 FC 533 [Zhang 2008].

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the RPD erred, citing Zhang 2008 that bribery can allow wanted persons to exit China on their own passport.

propositions.text: The Applicant claims he travelled with a snakehead and ten others but knows nothing about the other travellers.
propositions.quote: The Applicant claims that he travelled with the snakehead in a group with ten other people; however, the Applicant stated that he knows nothing about the ten other travellers and that he did not ask any of them about their backgrounds, despite the fact that they were all travelling to Toronto together.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant says he travelled with a snakehead and ten others but did not know their backgrounds.

propositions.text: The Applicant could not provide details about passport handling at check-in, security, or customs, recalling only a conversation about liquid limits.
propositions.quote: The Applicant also could not provide any details about what happened with his passport at the check-in counter, security screening, or customs. He merely stated that he did not observe whether or not his passport was scanned at the check-in counter to receive his boarding pass, similarly he did not see the security agent scan his passport. At the customs check point, the Applicant states that he presented his documents to the customs agent but does not remember what they did with the documents. The Applicant did not recall the snakehead directing him to a specific agent. Further, the only conversation that he could remember overhearing between the snakehead and any airport official was a discussion he believed to be about liquid limits for air travel.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant could not recall passport handling details at airport security and customs, only overhearing a conversation about liquid limits.

propositions.text: The RPD acknowledged snakehead could bribe officials but Applicant gave no evidence of special methods to evade security.
propositions.quote: The RPD was cognizant of the fact that a snakehead could make the requisite arrangements, including bribes, in order to successfully pass through Beijing airport with a person who is wanted by the PSB. However, the Applicant provided no evidence or testimony regarding special procedures or methods employed by the snakehead to enable the group to evade airport security measures;

propositions.text: The RPD inferred from the boarding pass in Applicant's name that his passport was scanned and travel subject to detection, justifying a negative credibility inference.
propositions.quote: and, by his own account, he followed a generally standard boarding procedure, as outlined in National Documentation Package. Further, the RPD concluded that it was reasonable to infer, from the fact that the Applicant’s boarding pass was in his own name, that the Applicant’s passport had been scanned, so that his travel would be subject to detection by the authorities. Base on all the above, the RPD held that it was appropriate to draw a negative credibility inference.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD recognized possible bribery but found no evidence of special evasion methods and inferred passport scanning, supporting negative credibility.

propositions.text: The court finds the RPD's decision reasonable, distinguishing this case from Zhang 2008 and aligning with Sui and Ma cases where claims were not credible.
propositions.quote: I find that the RPD’s decision was reasonable. While the Federal Court’s jurisprudence is mixed on the issue of exiting China under one’s own identity while being wanted by authorities, the circumstances here are more similar to cases such as Sui v Canada, 2016 FC 406, and Ma v Canada, 2015 FC 838, where the claimants’ allegations were not found credible. Further, the absence of a concrete explanation as to how the Applicant managed to evade the security measures at Beijing airport, distinguishes this case from Zhang 2008, above.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD's decision reasonable, distinguishing it from Zhang 2008 and aligning with cases rejecting similar claims.

propositions.text: The court agrees with the Respondent that the RPD reasonably drew a negative credibility finding after careful evidence consideration.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Respondent that the RPD carefully considered the evidence and reasonably drew a negative credibility finding based on the Applicant’s claim and the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with the Respondent that the RPD reasonably found the Applicant not credible after careful evidence review.

propositions.text: The RPD drew a negative credibility inference from the Applicant's claim that PSB officers visited his parents' home four times without leaving documentation.
propositions.quote: The RPD also drew a negative credibility inference upon the Applicant’s evidence that PSB officers attended his parents’ home on four occasions but did not leave any documentation to indicate their interest in him.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found it not credible that PSB officers visited the Applicant's parents four times without leaving documentation.

propositions.text: The Applicant argues it was unreasonable for the RPD to infer lack of credibility given inconsistent PSB summons practices in China.
propositions.quote: The Applicant argues that it was unreasonable for the RPD to draw a negative credibility inference based on this part his claim, because the RPD acknowledged that, at the relevant time, the practice of leaving a summons with family members was inconsistent in China.

propositions.text: The Applicant notes some cases found regional differences in PSB summons norms.
propositions.quote: However, the RPD inferred that a summons would have been left, based upon the number of PSB visits to the Applicant’s parents’ home. However, there are some cases where the Court found as a fact that the PSB in different regions may have different norms regarding when they leave summonses.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the RPD was unreasonable to infer lack of credibility given inconsistent PSB summons practices and regional differences.

propositions.text: The RPD relied on a 2015 Response to Information Request about summons regulations to find it unlikely PSB would visit four times without leaving any documentation.
propositions.quote: The RPD relied upon the Response to Information Request, dated October 20, 2015, regarding Regulations on summonses to inform the finding that it was not credible that the PSB would visit the Applicant’s parents four times and not leave a written summons.

propositions.text: Despite acknowledging inconsistencies, the RPD found it unlikely no documentary evidence would exist in this case.
propositions.quote: While acknowledging that there can be inconsistencies in the practice of issuing written summonses to family members, the RPD found that, in this case, it was unlikely that the PSB would not leave any documentary evidence whatsoever.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found it unlikely PSB would visit four times without leaving documentation, relying on a 2015 information response.

propositions.text: The RPD may assess plausibility and apply common sense in evaluating sworn testimony, citing Ye and Su cases.
propositions.quote: In assessing the sworn testimony of an applicant, the RPD is entitled to consider its plausibility and to apply common sense and rationality (Ye v Canada, 2014 FC 1221 at para 29; Su v Canada, 2015 FC 666 at para 11 [Su]).

propositions.text: It is reasonable for the RPD to find lack of credibility given absence of PSB documentation and other evidence.
propositions.quote: I find that it is reasonable, in the context of the surrounding evidence—in particular, the Applicant’s exit from China using his own passport—for the RPD to have found a lack of credibility given the absence of PSB documentation.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the RPD can assess plausibility and finds it reasonable to doubt credibility given no PSB documentation and other evidence.

propositions.text: RPD drew negative credibility inference due to Applicant's delay in claiming protection after arrival at airports
propositions.quote: The RPD drew a negative credibility inference upon the Applicant’s evidence that he fled China in fear of arrest, imprisonment, and physical harm as he did not claim for protection immediately upon his arrival at either the Vancouver or Toronto airports.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Applicant less credible for not claiming protection immediately upon arrival at Canadian airports.

propositions.text: Applicant argues delay in claim was brief and due to ignorance of refugee claim process
propositions.quote: The Applicant argues that this inference is unreasonable because the delay in making the claim was brief (approximately 34 days). Moreover, the Applicant argues that he did not make a refugee application immediately upon entering Canada because he did not know that he could make a refugee claim to stay in Canada permanently.

propositions.text: Applicant admitted he hoped Canadian government would protect him and knew about refugee system from a friend
propositions.quote: However, after being questioned about why he and his family would spend a large sum of money to hire a snakehead and obtain a fraudulent visa, the Applicant admitted that he came to Canada with the hope that the Canadian government would protect him. Further, he stated that the friend, in whose home he had been hiding in China, told him that Canada had a refugee system and that the Canadian government would help people such as him.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues delay was brief and due to ignorance but admitted hope for protection and knowledge of refugee system from a friend.

propositions.text: RPD's negative credibility inference on Applicant's knowledge and delay is reasonable given contradictory testimony
propositions.quote: Given the Applicant’s contradictory testimony regarding what he did and did not know about refugee claims in Canada, and when he knew such information, I find that the RPD’s decision to draw a negative credibility inference is reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RPD's negative credibility inference reasonable due to Applicant's contradictory testimony about refugee claim knowledge.

propositions.text: RPD drew negative credibility inference due to Applicant's fraudulent US visa attempt without compelling reason
propositions.quote: The RPD drew a general negative credibility inference upon the Applicant’s evidence because he attempted to obtain a US visa through fraudulent means in 2013, without a compelling reason for the misrepresentation.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found Applicant less credible for attempting fraudulent US visa without compelling reason.

propositions.text: Applicant argues RPD's negative inference on US visa fraud was unreasonable and irrelevant to refugee claim
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that it was unreasonable for the RPD to make this negative credibility inference because the misrepresentation on the US visa has nothing to do with the issue before RPD.

propositions.text: Applicant asserts credibility finding is not determinative of refugee status and relies on Guney case to argue one lie doesn't discredit all evidence
propositions.quote: The Applicant asserts that “a finding that a refugee claimant is or is not credible is not determinative of the question of whether that claimant is a convention refugee.” Further, the Applicant relies upon the case Guney v Canada, 2008 FC 1134 [Guney], for the proposition that the fact that a witness has been caught in a lie is insufficient to discredit all of his or her evidence, where the evidence is otherwise plausible.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues RPD's negative inference on US visa fraud was irrelevant and cites Guney to say one lie doesn't discredit all evidence.

propositions.text: Court finds RPD did not discredit otherwise plausible evidence due to US visa fraud and evidence was not otherwise plausible
propositions.quote: I do not find that the RPD applied this general negative credibility finding to discredit otherwise plausible evidence or to simply dismiss the remainder of the Applicant’s testimony. Unlike the situation in Guney, above, the evidence with regard to the Applicant’s Falun Gong practice, persecution, and flight is not “otherwise plausible and consistent” (Guney at para 17).

propositions.text: RPD did not disregard other evidence due to fraudulent visa; misrepresentation casts doubt without corroboration
propositions.quote: The RPD did not disregard any of the other evidence because of the fraudulent US visa application. This is a case where evidence of a willingness to make misrepresentations to immigration officials can cast doubt on the Applicant’s testimony, particularly where there is no corroborating evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RPD reasonably doubted Applicant's testimony due to visa fraud and lack of corroboration, unlike Guney case.

propositions.text: RPD found Applicant's evidence on Falun Gong practice not persuasive to establish genuine practitioner status
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the Applicant’s evidence regarding his practice of Falun Gong was not persuasive in establishing that he is a genuine Falun Gong practitioner.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found Applicant's Falun Gong practice evidence unpersuasive to prove genuine practice.

propositions.text: Applicant argues RPD unreasonably scrutinized his Falun Gong knowledge and failed to give reasons for rejecting explanations about not owning Zhuan Falun
propositions.quote: The Applicant argues that the RPD wrongly engaged in a microscopic and stringent examination of the Applicant’s knowledge of Falun Gong. Further, the Applicant asserts that it was unreasonable for the RPD to make a negative finding based upon the Applicant’s failure to obtain a copy of Zhuan Falun, the central text for Falun Gong practitioners, as he is a person of limited education, who would not understand most of the text. The Applicant also contends that it is unreasonable that the RPD did not give reasons for rejecting the Applicant’s explanations of why he does not own a copy of Zhuan Falun.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues RPD unreasonably scrutinized his Falun Gong knowledge and failed to explain rejecting his reasons for not owning Zhuan Falun.

propositions.text: RPD found Applicant's reasons for joining Falun Gong lacked cogency and he failed to describe principles or obtain Zhuan Falun
propositions.quote: The RPD determined that the Applicant’s reasons for joining Falun Gong, which he knew was illegal and could lead to persecution, lacked cogency. Further, he could not describe why any of the principles of Falun Gong had personal appeal to him and could only discuss the benefits of Falun Gong practice in a very general manner. The RPD also found that the Applicant’s failure to obtain a copy of Zhuan Falun, once in Canada, due to an apparent lack of effort on his part, detracted from his credibility that he was a genuine practitioner.

propositions.text: RPD inferred genuine practitioner would have tried to obtain Zhuan Falun in Canada despite no explicit reasons rejecting Applicant's explanation
propositions.quote: Although, the RPD did not give explicit reasons for rejecting the Applicant’s explanation of why he does not own a copy of Zhuan Falun, it can be inferred from the RPD’s reasons that a genuine practitioner—who was coming to Canada, a place where the practice of Falun Gong is legal, to study and practice Falun Gong—would have made efforts to obtain a copy of the text so that he could further his understanding.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found Applicant's Falun Gong reasons unconvincing and inferred genuine practitioners would seek Zhuan Falun in Canada.

propositions.text: Respondent made misstatements about Applicant's gender and story inconsistent with this case
propositions.quote: However, certain of the Respondent’s submissions on this issue appear to be from a different case. In one instance, the Respondent refers to the Applicant as “her”, and makes reference to a story about the Applicant fleeing the PSB raid, and hiding in a field.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes Respondent's misstatements about Applicant's gender and story inconsistent with this case.

propositions.text: Despite Respondent's errors, RPD reasonably found Applicant not a genuine Falun Gong practitioner due to lack of corroboration and disinterest in Zhuan Falun
propositions.quote: Nevertheless, notwithstanding the Respondent’s misstatements referred to above on this issue, I find that the RPD made a reasonable finding that the Applicant is not a genuine Falun Gong practitioner. In particular, I find that the lack of corroborating evidence and the Applicant’s apparently disinterest in obtaining a copy of Zhuan Falun, despite his testimony that he is here in Canada because he wants to practice Falun Gong and improve his life, supports a lack of credibility.

propositions.text: Other RPD credibility findings are cogent and determinative
propositions.quote: In any event, the other credibility findings by the RPD are cogent and determinative.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RPD reasonably concluded Applicant not genuine Falun Gong practitioner despite Respondent's errors; other credibility findings decisive.

propositions.text: RPD concluded insufficient evidence that Chinese authorities will persecute Applicant for Falun Gong activities in Canada
propositions.quote: The RPD considered whether the Applicant’s alleged participation in Falun Gong in Canada has come or will come to the attention of the Chinese authorities and whether the Applicant will face more than a mere possibility of persecution as a result (Liu v Canada, 2014 FC 972 at para 8). The RPD concluded that because there is insufficient evidence to show that the Applicant is a Falun Gong practitioner in Canada, it follows that there is insufficient evidence to establish that the Chinese authorities will take an interest in the Applicant because of his alleged Canadian Falun Gong activities.

propositions.text: Court agrees with RPD's conclusion on insufficient evidence of persecution risk from Canadian Falun Gong activities
propositions.quote: I agree.

paragraphs.summary: RPD and court agree insufficient evidence shows Chinese authorities will persecute Applicant for Canadian Falun Gong activities.

propositions.text: Court finds RPD's decision reasonable and dismisses application with no certification question
propositions.quote: Based upon the evidence before me, I find that the RPD’s decision was reasonable. JUDGMENT in IMM-4882-16 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that The application is dismissed. There is no question for certification.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RPD decision reasonable and dismisses application with no certification question.
